[[CHAPTER 2]{.calibre4}]{.calibre9}\
[[[CHRIST, FULLNESS OF THE]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre24}\
[[[ REVELATION OF GOD]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre24}

> [After God had spoken many times and in various ways through the
> prophets, "in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son"
> (Heb 1: 2). For he sent his Son, the eternal Word who enlightens all
> men, to dwell among men and to tell them about the inner life of God.
> Hence, Jesus Christ . . . "utters the words of God" (Jn 3: 34), and
> accomplishes the saving work that the Father gave him to do
> (cf. Jn 5: 36; 17: 4). As a result, he himself---to see whom is to see
> the Father (cf. Jn 14: 9)---completed and perfected revelation and
> confirmed it with divine guarantees. He did this by the total fact of
> his presence and self-manifestation---by words and works, signs and
> miracles, but above all by his death and glorious Resurrection from
> the dead, and finally by sending the Spirit of Truth. He revealed that
> God was with us, to deliver us from the darkness of sin and death, and
> to raise us up to eternal
> life.^[[[1]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[In this way, Vatican II describes the various issues raised by
affirming that Christ is the plenitude of revelation, while it stresses
the intimate and essential relationship between revelation and
salvation. Let us carefully read the initial text of the Letter to
Hebrews briefly cited in the above text.]{.calibre4}

> [In many and various ways God spoke of old to our fathers by the
> prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he
> appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the
> world. He reflects the glory of God and bears the very stamp of his
> nature, upholding the universe by his word of power. When he had made
> purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on
> high, having become as much superior to angels as the name he has
> obtained is more excellent than theirs. (Heb 1: 1-- 4)]{.calibre4}

[These initial verses in St. Paul's Letter to the Hebrews summarize the
history of salvation. They are a clear expression of the
]{.calibre4}[[plenitude]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ that revelation, united
intimately to salvation itself, has in Christ, eternal Word of God, Son
of God made man. Hebrews presents Jesus as the culmination of historical
revelation and of history itself. The reference to the work of creation
leads us to consider the mystery of Christ as the plenitude of the
cosmic revelation.]{.calibre4}

> [The mystery of Christ, as Son of God made Man, shows a new and very
> particular event about the divine manifestations of the past. . . . It
> is a unique and absolute fact that sets itself apart from what had
> been revealed before and situates itself as the beginning of a
> completely new and unprecedented relation of filial communion of man
> with God. . . . Therefore, while we consider Christ as the conclusion
> and plenitude of revelation, we have to avoid the error of considering
> him in the same existential line as the Old Testament. We have to
> consider Christ for what he really is, as an absolutely new event,
> without diminishing the preparatory purpose of the
> old.^[[[2]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[[[I. Christ, Fullness of the Creative
Word]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[The affirmation, "Christ is the plenitude of the creative Word," has a
rich and diverse meaning. It signifies that Christ possesses perfect
humanity because it is the humanity of God, and God is perfect. In the
glorious Christ, therefore, all created things are destined to attain to
the new heaven and the new earth.]{.calibre4}

[All things have been created because of Christ. He is heir to all
things, and not only because he is and always will be the universal
Lord. All created things---all in their own way---are destined to
constitute a certain glorious unity with Christ at the end of history in
such way that "God may be everything to every one"
(1 Cor 15: 28).]{.calibre4}

[Nature does not require grace. The "new creation" is not the result of
the development or evolution of the first creation. Yet, according to
the plan of God, the first creation is destined from the beginning to
become the second and definitive one.]{.calibre4}

[[[A. Creation Has Been Made in View of
Christ]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[In the aforementioned text (Heb 1: 1-- 4), St. Paul speaks of a double
dimension between created things and Christ: God "has made the world
through his Son," and he "has named Christ heir of all things." The
first aspect of this relationship refers, obviously, to Christ as God
(the eternal Word before the Incarnation). The second refers,
undoubtedly, to Christ as the Incarnate Word. In fact, it is only as man
that Christ is "heir of all things" (]{.calibre4}[[kleronomon
pantón]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[), since it is only as a man that Christ
"has inherited" (]{.calibre4}[[kekléronomekén]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[)
that excellent name which is referred to in Hebrews 1: 4: This name is
]{.calibre4}[[Kyrios]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (the Lord)
(cf. Phil 2: 9).]{.calibre4}

[Considering the first aspect, we learn the following: ]{.calibre4}[[God
carried out creation "by means of his Son."]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
St. John writes, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with
God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God; all things
were made through him, and without him was made nothing that was made"
(Jn 1: 1-- 3).]{.calibre4}

[The work of creation is common to the three divine Persons. Thus, the
expression "through him (the Word)" cannot be understood in an
instrumental sense. In order to comprehend the meaning of the above
passage, we must take into account the following words of St. Paul: "He
is the image of the invisible God, the first-born of all creation; for
in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth. . . . He is
before all things, and in him all things hold together" (Col 1: 15--
16a, 17).^[[[3]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Although this creative power belongs to the entire Trinity, we must
affirm that a special relationship exists between created things and the
Logos. Thus, St. Thomas Aquinas writes, "The Son, from the very fact
that he is the Word which perfectly expresses the Father, expresses all
of creation."^[[[4]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Elsewhere (and
more concisely), he states that the Word is the "efficient cause of the
things that God
creates."^[[[5]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Logos is the eternal Word of God. But in some way, it is also the Word
manifested to creatures. In any event, creatures have this special
relationship with the Logos inasmuch as ]{.calibre4}[[this relationship
manifests the divine nature]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. Consequently, this
relationship does not give man the possibility of a natural knowledge of
the Trinity by means of creatures. This relationship of creatures with
the divine Logos has the same root as the
]{.calibre4}[[logic]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of the
world^[[[6]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^: of its truth, its
intelligibility, and, therefore, its being the starting point of man's
natural knowledge of God. In this vein, certain Church Fathers wrote
about the presence of the Word in the world before the Incarnation
(particularly St. Justin and
St. Irenaeus).^[[[7]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[It is clear that St. John, in the expression
]{.calibre4}[[di'autou]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (Jn 1: 2), referred to the
Word in its eternal pre-existence before the Incarnation. St. Paul also
referred to Christ as the God-Man (]{.calibre4}[[en
autó]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[: Col 1: 16-- 17) in his divinity. However,
St. Paul emphasized Christ as God acting in the creation and
conservation of the world.]{.calibre4}

[Let us now consider another aspect of the relationship between Christ
and the whole of creation, one taken from the beginning of the Letter to
the Hebrews: ]{.calibre4}[[Christ has inherited
everything]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. Christ has been ordained Lord of all
creation. Nevertheless, we must point out another important facet of
this issue indicated by St. Paul in the Letter to the Colossians: "All
things were created through him and for him \[]{.calibre4}[[ta panta
di'autou kai eis autom ektistai]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[\]" (Col 1: 16).
In the Vulgate, the translation is ]{.calibre4}[[omnia per ipsum et in
ipso creata sunt]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. In the Neo-Vulgate this passage
is translated in a more precise manner: ]{.calibre4}[[omnia per ipsum et
in ipsum creata sunt]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, expressing in this way the
dynamic sense of finality that in Greek the
]{.calibre4}[[ein]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ has with the accusative, which
corresponds in Latin with the ]{.calibre4}[[in]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of
the accusative.]{.calibre4}

[Therefore, in this text (Col 1: 16b), St. Paul---in addition to
reaffirming that creation was carried out through the Word
(]{.calibre4}[[di'autou]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[)---affirmed that creation
was carried out ]{.calibre4}[[because of Christ]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.
In the exegesis, the interpretations are not unanimous as to whether the
Apostle was talking about Christ just in his divinity, in his divinity
and humanity, or in his being God-Man. The most commonly held and best
grounded opinion is that the expression ]{.calibre4}[[eis
autum]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ refers to Christ as God made Man, because
St. Paul says soon thereafter, "He is the head of the body, the church;
he is the beginning, the first-born from the dead, that in everything he
might be pre-eminent" (Col 1: 18). This passage, evidently, does not
refer to Christ only in his divinity, but in his mystery of
God-Man.^[[[8]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Consequently, we can state that the ]{.calibre4}[[cosmic
revelation---creation---was carried out in preparation for the
Incarnation of the personal Word of God: in preparation for the coming
of Christ.]{.calibre4}]{.italic}

[There is no necessary connection between creation and Incarnation, but
God apparently wished and foresaw such a relationship "before creation."
"Before creation," the free divine plan included all human history:
creation, sin, and redeeming Incarnation with or without the fall of
man.^[[[9]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[[[B. The Humanity of Christ, Fullness of
Creation]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[Christ, in his humanity, is the plenitude of the Word of creation; He
is the plenitude of creation. The Word of creation reveals God in man,
because man was created "in our image, after our likeness" (Gen 1: 26).
Christ is the ]{.calibre4}[[perfect man, the new
Adam]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. He is not made to the likeness of the first
Adam because Adam was the one who was "a type of the one who was to
come" (Rom 5: 14), the Lord
Christ.^[[[10]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

> [He who is the "image of the invisible God" (Col 1: 15), is himself
> the perfect man who has restored in the children of Adam that likeness
> to God that had been disfigured since the first sin. Human nature, by
> the very fact that it was assumed in him, not absorbed, has also been
> raised in us to incomparable
> dignity.^[[[11]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The humanity of Jesus is the supreme expression of the word of
creation. Christ reveals his perfect humanity to man, and, in addition,
he shows mankind the unity of his divine Person, ]{.calibre4}[[the same
eternal Word of God]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ made visible in flesh. In
other words, his human nature is ]{.calibre4}[[the humanity of
God]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, and, therefore, it is "]{.calibre4}[[a way
of being]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of God: the way of being not divine that
the Son of God has taken for
himself."^[[[12]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The fact that the
humanity of Christ is true (not divine) humanity does not diminish its
character as a ]{.calibre4}[[way of being of God]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
and, therefore, a manifestation of God. Here we may draw the analogy of
a musical instrument that has a distinct nature from the one who plays
it. "Everything Christ did has a transcendental value. It shows us the
nature of God."^[[[13]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The Lord
himself asserted with great clarity, "He who has seen me has seen the
Father" (Jn 14: 9).]{.calibre4}

[In this way St. John, inspired by God, was able to say about Christ,
"And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth;
we have beheld his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father"
(Jn 1: 14 ). The term ]{.calibre4}[[glory]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(]{.calibre4}[[doxa]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ in Greek,
]{.calibre4}[[kabod]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ in Hebrew) means the divine
being as he manifests himself to
men.^[[[14]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[St. John also wrote, "That which was from the beginning, which we have
heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and
touched with our hands, concerning the word of life . . . we proclaim
also to you" (1 Jn 1: 1, 3). There have been several interpretations of
this text claiming that the phrase "the word of life" might not refer to
the divine Person of the Word. Yet, it would seem most logical for
St. John to use the term ]{.calibre4}[[logos]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ to
refer to Christ in a personal sense rather than to use the term logos
for some other
purpose.^[[[15]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[[[C. The New Creation in Christ]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[Christ, whose humanity is "full of grace and truth" (Jn 1: 14), is also
revelation because he is the divine Word that means and carries out
supernatural salvation, which is a ]{.calibre4}[[new
creation]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (cf. Gal 6: 15;
2 Cor 5: 17).]{.calibre4}

[Above all, Christ, who has risen and is seated at the right hand of the
Father, is the plenitude of the Word of creation, "For in him the whole
fullness of deity dwells bodily \[]{.calibre4}[[en autó katoikei pan to
pléróma tés theotétos sómatikós]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[\]" (Col 2: 9).
This text, although directly understood as an affirmation of the
Incarnation (the personal union of divinity and humanity in Jesus),
refers particularly to the complete glorification (deification) of the
most holy humanity of Christ after his Resurrection and
Ascension.^[[[16]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Moreover, the
glorification of the body of Christ, which we consider a proper and
authentic---although mysterious---]{.calibre4}[[deification of
matter]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, may be due to an ontologically prior
spiritualization of matter (cf. 1 Cor 15: 44): a new manner of uniting
body and soul that confers quasi-spiritual properties upon the body and
that, in addition, implies that the resurrected Christ is
]{.calibre4}[[immortal]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ in the strict sense of the
word (cf. Rom 6: 9;
1 Cor 15: 23).^[[[17]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[This plenitude of the Word of creation that manifests itself in the
totally glorified holy humanity of Jesus will produce ]{.calibre4}[[the
new heaven and the new earth]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ at the end of
history (cf. Rom 8: 19-- 23; 2 Pt 3: 13; Rv 21: 1). Visible creation
]{.calibre4}[[will be called forth anew]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, because
of the divine plan "to unite all things in him
\[]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósasthai ta panta en tó
Christó]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[\]" (Eph 1: 10). Thus, the glorious Church
will be "the fullness of him who fills all in all" (Eph 1: 23) because
the glorious Christ will fill all things (cf. Eph 4: 10) and because
these participate in his plenitude (cf. Col 2: 9).]{.calibre4}

[The exegesis of this
]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ or
]{.calibre4}[[recapitulation]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of everything in
Christ has had a long and rich history. The etymology seems clear: It
comes from ]{.calibre4}[[ana]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (as a verb prefix
means "again," or "re-" in addition to meaning "upward," or "backward";
and from ]{.calibre4}[[kephalaion]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ ("chapter" or
"summit"). Nevertheless, the precise meaning of the term
]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósasthai]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ in the text of
Ephesians 1: 10 is not entirely clear. In any case, the translation of
the Neo-Vulgate is preferable to that of the Vulgate
(]{.calibre4}[[recapitulare omnia in Christo]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[).
St. Paul uses this term on another occasion to indicate that all of the
law is ]{.calibre4}[[recapitulated]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaioutai]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) in the double
precept of charity (cf. Rom 13: 9).]{.calibre4}

[Among the Greek Fathers, St. Irenaeus stressed the importance of
Ephesians 1: 10, considering the recapitulation of all things in Christ
as finality of the ]{.calibre4}[[parousia]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
together with the resurrection of humanity and the universal
judgment.^[[[18]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Further, the exegesis
of St. John Chrysostom, St. Theodoret of Cyrrhus and St. John Damascene
are particularly important on this topic.]{.calibre4}

[St. John Chrysostom indicates two meanings of the term
]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. The first and more
direct is "recapitulation," understood as a brief summary of all that
has been previously said (taking into consideration that the term
derives from ]{.calibre4}[[kephalaion]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[). In this
sense, Ephesians 1: 10 means that everything that God had previously
made for the salvation of the world is contained in
Christ.^[[[19]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Then, Chrysostom
immediately adds that
]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ has another
meaning: "to assign a head again" or "to reinstate as head" (based on
the term deriving from ]{.calibre4}[[kephalé]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[).
That is why, according to him, in Ephesians 1: 10, St. Paul also speaks
of placing Christ as head of all terrestrial and celestial
creatures.^[[[20]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ In this context it
may be deduced that the terrestrial and celestial beings to whom
St. Paul refers are angels and men, but one cannot exclude the fact that
he attributes to ]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ a
more universal sense that really comprehends all that has been
created.]{.calibre4}

[St. Theodoret of Cyrrhus was the one who most explicitly interpreted
]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ in a cosmic
universal sense. According to him, at the end of history everyone will
be gathered under Christ, who will be the head not only of angels and
men but also of the entire universe, which will be transformed and
become incorruptible. In that sense, Theodoret interprets
Ephesians 1: 10 together with Romans 8: 19-- 22: "The whole creation has
been groaning in travail until
now."^[[[21]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[St. John Damascene took a third exegetical position, seeing
]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ as "restoration."
He interpreted St. Paul as teaching in Ephesians 1: 10 that at the end
of history Christ will restore angels and men to a primitive state of
happiness and sanctity (not in the sense of ]{.calibre4}[[apokatastasis
pantón]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ suggested by Origen, but in the sense of
canceling the mourning that exists even in heaven---among
angels---through the complete salvation of just
men).^[[[22]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[This interpretation of Damacene's was very common among the Latin
Fathers, mainly because in the versions of Scripture they possessed,
]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósasthai]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ had been
translated as ]{.calibre4}[[to restore]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ or
]{.calibre4}[[to establish]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. ]{.calibre4}\

[For instance, St. Augustine wrote about the "restoration" of men and
angels (in the sense that the number of fallen angels will be restored
through the men that will be
saved).^[[[23]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ St. Jerome, among the
Latin Fathers, interpreted this passage according to the sense of the
Greek text and translated
]{.calibre4}[[anakephalaiósasthai]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ as
]{.calibre4}[[to recapitulate]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (as Tertullian had
already done), thereby giving the same explanation as St. John
Chrysostom.^[[[24]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The medieval exegetes principally depended on the Latin Fathers for the
translation of Ephesians 1: 10, where they found ]{.calibre4}[[to
restore]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ or also ]{.calibre4}[[to
establish]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. Thus, their possible interpretations
were limited. St. Thomas Aquinas felt that the text, when it says
]{.calibre4}[[instaurare omnia in Christo]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, refers
not only to angels and men but to the whole cosmos as well. The final
destiny of the universe depends on the destiny of man because everything
that was created is according to
man.^[[[25]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[In his commentary on Romans 8: 19, St. Thomas Aquinas referred to
Revelation 21: 1 and wrote of a cosmic recapitulation of creation. The
eschatological glorification will encompass not only the human body but
also the whole cosmos.^[[[26]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Thus,
the whole creation will truly constitute a certain glorious unity with
angels and men in Christ and under Christ.]{.calibre4}

[Contemporary exegesis offers different directions of interpretation in
this area that can be considered complementary and that coincide
substantially with some already posited by the Church
Fathers.^[[[27]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[In summary, we can say:]{.calibre4}

> [["To restore all things in Christ"]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ should be
> interpreted in the sense that God (the Father) gives all things,
> celestial and terrestrial, the whole creation, to one sole head, who
> is Jesus Christ. Christ, therefore, is head of the Church
> (cf. Eph 1: 22), which is ]{.calibre4}[[his body and his
> plenitude]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (cf. Eph 1: 23). In other words,
> Christ is head of the universe, but especially of the Church. The
> whole universe is placed under Christ, is unified in him and elevated
> in him.^[[[28]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[This "elevation" of the whole creation into the "glorious Christ"
entails a supernatural transformation of the entire cosmos into a "new
creation." The transformation will be the plenitude of the creating Word
(also as revelation) because it will constitute an "adjustment" of the
visible world to the senses of the resurrected man. This is what
St. Thomas boldly and deeply explained as the ]{.calibre4}[[lumen
gloriae]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.^[[[29]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Of course, this "new creation in Christ," as the plenitude of the
creating Word, will be carried out fully only at the end of history.
Still, it has already been partially accomplished in the humanity of
Jesus Christ. Therefore, the definitive state of the "new creation" will
not be something completely new. The
]{.calibre4}[[recapitulation]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of everything in the
glorious Christ (cf. Eph 1: 10) will complete what the Incarnation
started: "The 'firstborn of all creation' (Col 1: 15) becoming incarnate
in the individual humanity of Christ, unites himself in someway with the
entire reality of man, which is also 'flesh' (cf., i.e., Gen 9: 11;
Dt 5: 26; Jb 34: 15; Is 40: 6; 52: 10; Ps 145: 21; Lk 3: 6; 1 Pt 1: 24)
--- and in this reality with all 'flesh,' with the whole of
creation."^[[[30]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Between creation and the "new creation," there is discontinuity because
the "new creation" is not the consequence of an immanent evolution.
There is also a certain continuity because the first creation is not to
be destroyed, but transformed (cf. Rom 8: 19-- 22; 2 Pt 3: 7--
13).]{.calibre4}

[[[II. Christ, Fullness of the Word of the
Covenant]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[In the covenant, God established a relationship with mankind: a union
that, naturally, did not diminish in any way God's transcendence over
man. In Christ we see a definitive and perfect covenant carried out: he
is, really, true God and true man in a personal unity (cf. Jer 31: 31--
34; 1 Cor 11: 25). In him, the divine nature and human nature are united
in the most intimate and definitive way imaginable while simultaneously
remaining distinct.^[[[31]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Moreover, the covenant was a relationship based in love that is
presented in the Old Testament as
]{.calibre4}[[adoption]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[---Israel is adopted as
God's son (cf. Ex 4: 22; Hos 11: 1)---and as the ]{.calibre4}[[marriage
union]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (cf. Is 54: 5-- 8; Ez 16). In this manner,
the promised Incarnation is treated as the fulfillment of the covenant.
In fact, it is in Christ that mankind acquires the plenitude of divine
sonship because in him there is no simple
adoption.^[[[32]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The comparison
between the covenant of God and the people of Israel via the marital
union reaches its fullness in Christ because he is the Spouse of the
Church (cf. Eph 5: 25-- 27, 32).]{.calibre4}

[Consequently, Christ carries out the fullness of the covenant. In him
the meaning of revelation regarding the covenant reaches its plenitude.
In fact, the old covenant was mainly a revelation, in human history, of
the truth and fidelity, justice, and love of God. It is in Christ that
the perfect manifestation of God to mankind takes place, of his perfect
fidelity to his promises, of his supreme justice united with mercy, as
demonstrated, above all, in the sacrifice of the
cross.^[[[33]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Naturally, just as the Old Testament reveals, in addition to the love
and the faithfulness of God, many other things about God and
man^[[[34]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^, so in Christ is the
supreme fulfillment of the divine revelation realized in all its
multiform content, especially about God in his Trinity of Persons, and
about man. In fact, Christ is the "fullness because he expresses the
mystery of the Father and works with the power of the
Spirit."^[[[35]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ "Christ, who is the
new Adam, by revealing the mystery of the Father and of His love, fully
reveals man to man, and manifests to him his highest
vocation."^[[[36]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The covenant had, as its essential elements, the ]{.calibre4}[[Promise
and the Law]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. Let us now consider how in Christ
the Promise, is completely fulfilled, and how in him the Law reaches its
perfection, becoming a perfect law of liberty.]{.calibre4}

[In Christ, ]{.calibre4}[[the Promise reaches its complete
fulfillment]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. Among the promises made to Abraham
by God, those that referred to the descendants of Abraham, their
establishment as a great people---through liberation from the Egyptian
yoke---and that of giving his people the promised land, had already been
fulfilled in the history prior to Christ. But only with the Incarnation
is the Promise completely fulfilled with respect to universal salvation,
that is, only through Christ and in Christ is the word given by God to
Abraham fulfilled: "And by your descendants shall all the nations of the
earth bless themselves" (Gen 22: 18; cf. Gal 3: 16, 26--
29).]{.calibre4}

[Through the Incarnation, the Law also reaches its perfection and
fullness.]{.calibre4}

> [Christ instituted this new covenant, namely the new covenant in his
> blood (cf. 1 Cor 11: 25); he called a race made up of Jews and
> Gentiles that would be one, not according to the flesh, but in the
> Spirit, and this race would be the new people of God. For those who
> believe in Christ, who are reborn, not from a corruptible seed, but
> from an incorruptible one through the word of the living God
> (cf. 1 Pt 1: 23), not from flesh, but from water and the Holy Spirit
> (cf. Jn 3: 5-- 6), are finally established as "a chosen race, a royal
> priesthood, a holy nation," who in times past were "no people" but now
> are "God's people" (1 Pt 2: 9--
> 10).^[[[37]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Christ, therefore, is the perfect covenant in himself, and in him all
of the promises are completely fulfilled: the new people of God is
constituted; it is universal in nature, and it is freed from the slavery
of sin by the new Passover to be sons of God (cf. Rom 8: 21). By means
of the Incarnation, the ]{.calibre4}[[law also reaches its perfection
and fullness]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. The issue of the relationship
between the old law and the new law is presented in several books of the
New Testament in ways that though articulate, sometimes do not lend
themselves to easy
interpretation.^[[[38]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The purpose of the law is to teach and encourage men to lead just
lives. Consequently, the law of the Old Testament itself could not
justify men; it could only present and promise justice. According to the
words of the Apostle: "For God has done what the law, weakened by the
flesh, could not do: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh
and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the just
requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us" (Rom 8: 3--
4).^[[[39]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The new law does not merely
teach what is just and unjust. It also carries an ]{.calibre4}[[inner
grace]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ that gives one strength to
]{.calibre4}[[act in justice]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[: "The New Law is the
grace of the Holy Spirit, that is given to the
faithful."^[[[40]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ In this sense we can
understand the aforementioned text of Jeremiah (cf. Jer 31: 31-- 34), in
which is announced, as characteristic of the times of the future
covenant, a ]{.calibre4}[[law carved by God in the hearts of
men]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. In its concrete moral precepts, Christ
carried out the old law to its fulfillment and plenitude, especially by
his teaching. For it was Christ who explained the true sense of its
precepts (for instance, extending them to the intentions of men's hearts
\[cf. Mt 5: 20\]). It was Christ who directed their accomplishment
toward the perfect way (for example, in relation to oaths
\[cf. Mt 5: 33\]).^[[[41]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Another important aspect of this issue is that the law of Christ is
]{.calibre4}[[the perfect law of freedom]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(]{.calibre4}[[ho nomos teleios tes eleutherias]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[)
(cf. Jas 1: 25). St. Paul even went so far as to write, "For freedom
Christ has set us free; stand fast therefore, and do not submit again to
a yoke of slavery" (Gal 5: 1). Because of the context, it is obvious
that St. Paul makes a distinction between the old law, understood as the
law of slavery, and the new one, understood as the law of freedom. The
reason he drew this distinction is this: the new law is essentially
]{.calibre4}[[the law of grace and charity]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(cf. Gal 5: 4-- 14). In the same way, St. Paul presents the distinction
between the old law, which is
]{.calibre4}[[letter]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (cf. Rom 7: 6), and the law
of Christ, which is a law of the spirit (cf. Rom 8: 2). To the Gentiles,
the Apostle emphasized the connection between spirit and liberty: "Where
the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom" (2 Cor 3: 17). In this
text, "Spirit" does not seem to refer to the Person of the Holy Spirit,
but to the "spirit of Christ," understood as the inner world of the
grace of Christ in the spirit of redeemed
man.^[[[42]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The "law of Christ is freedom"---that is the paradox of Paul's message
in the Letter to the Galatians. This freedom has content, then, it has
direction, and it therefore contradicts what only apparently liberates
man, but in truth makes him a slave. The "Torah of the Messiah" is
totally new and different---but it is precisely by being such that it
fulfills the Torah of
Moses.^[[[43]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The relationship between grace, charity, and liberty that allows the
new law to be a "perfect law of freedom" is skillfully expressed by
St. Augustine in his famous words "Love and do whatever you
wish,"^[[[44]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ and "There is no chain
that coerces because freedom belongs to
love."^[[[45]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Similarly, St. Thomas
Aquinas wrote, "Insofar as a man has more charity, he has more
freedom."^[[[46]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Complete freedom is dependent on charity (]{.calibre4}[[libertas est
caritatis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) because freedom is a person's capacity
to love the good itself. It involves a person's ability to choose
correctly among different goods, without any coercion of the will. It is
in this arena that the love of God reaches its complete fulfillment. As
we know, the spirit of charity should inform the life of Christians in
such a way that they do everything out of love. It is not possible to
love without freedom.^[[[47]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ In other
words, the new law is a law of perfect freedom, not just because it
commands us ]{.calibre4}[[to love]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[---the old law
also commanded the same---but, primarily, because it gives us the
strength (]{.calibre4}[[charity]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) to
love.^[[[48]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[[[III. Christ, Fullness of the Prophetic
Word]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[Inasmuch as the prophetic Word is the Word of God in human form, it is,
in itself and forever, a preparation for the Incarnation of the eternal
Word. But in the Old Testament, the prophetic Word is also and
principally the preparation of the Incarnation of God, because when it
announces salvation it announces Christ implicitly and, oftentimes,
explicitly. Such is the case, for example, in the
]{.calibre4}[[messianic prophecies]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.]{.calibre4}

[Christ is the plenitude of the prophetic Word because he himself is the
]{.calibre4}[[perfect Prophet]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, not only because
in him prophecies are fulfilled. Above all, he is the
]{.calibre4}[[Master]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. In fact, the Old Testament
announced that the Messiah would be a great prophet. For instance, God
said to Moses, "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among
their brethren; and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak
to them all that I command him" (Dt 18: 18). Through Isaiah, God
announced the Messiah with these words: "Behold, I made him a witness to
the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples" (Is 55: 4). The
contemporaries of Jesus expected a Messiah who was also "the Prophet,"
although not everybody clearly saw the identification between "the
Prophet" and "the Messiah" (cf. Jn 1: 21-- 25).]{.calibre4}

[Undoubtedly, Jesus was sent by the Father as a
]{.calibre4}[[prophet]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ to convey the divine word
to humanity. He taught with divine authority. The Father himself, in
fact, commanded all to listen to Jesus' words (cf. Mt 17: 5). Christ
declared the plenitude of his teaching about God, assuring the exclusive
relationship of complete knowledge between him and the Father. "All
things have been delivered to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son
except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and any
one to whom the Son chooses to reveal him" (Mt 11: 27).]{.calibre4}

[However, Jesus is more than a prophet. He is the
]{.calibre4}[[Master]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (]{.calibre4}[[Rabbi,
didaskalos]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) who teaches with his own authority,
because he is Man and God in a personal unity (cf. Mt 7: 29; Jn 13: 13).
This authority, shown by Christ when he teaches, is strongly expressed
in the words "I say to you" (cf. Mt 5: 22, 28, 39;
Jn 8: 51).^[[[49]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ That is why
]{.calibre4}[[in Christo Deus docet
immediate^[[[50]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[;
Christ's words are the ]{.calibre4}[[human words of
God]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.]{.calibre4}

[Another aspect of Christ's prophetic function that manifests its
plenitude is the following: Jesus is concurrently the One that teaches
(Master) and the Truth that is taught. ]{.calibre4}[[He is the
Truth]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (cf. Jn 14: 6). Therefore, since he is the
]{.calibre4}[[Mediator]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ regarding the Truth
(Master and Prophet), his mediation is perfect (being the fullness of
prophetic mediation). This is true because it is the ]{.calibre4}[[most
immediate possible mediation]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[: "In the mediator
Christ we immediately find
God."^[[[51]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Finally, we ought to remember that Christ reveals not only with his
human words, but also in himself with all his works:
]{.calibre4}[[gestis
verbisque]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.^[[[52]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^
Therefore, as we have already noted, simply to see Christ is to see the
Father (cf. Jn 14: 9).]{.calibre4}

[[[IV. The Fullness of Revelation and the Fullness of
Time]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[Christ is the plenitude of revelation "because after him and above him
there is no more to tell, because in him God has revealed
himself."^[[[53]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Therefore, there will
not be another revelation of God after Christ; the ]{.calibre4}[[new
covenant is definitive]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. "The Christian economy,
therefore, since it is the new and definitive covenant, will never pass
away; and no new public revelation is to be expected before the glorious
manifestation of our Lord, Jesus Christ (cf. 1 Tm 6: 14;
Ti 2: 13)."^[[[54]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The historical
nature of revelation requires that the fullness of revelation entail a
plenitude of history, in other words, ]{.calibre4}[[a plenitude of
times]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.]{.calibre4}

[In the New Testament, two of the terms used that relate to temporality
are particularly relevant to the matter under consideration. The first
is ]{.calibre4}[[kronos]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (similar to the Hebrew
]{.calibre4}[[eth]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[), which points to
]{.calibre4}[[time]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ generically without a special
meaning, what we could call ]{.calibre4}[[quantitative
time]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, or simple duration. Secondly, we have
]{.calibre4}[[kairos]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (similar to the Hebrew
]{.calibre4}[[zemán]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[), which means "opportune
time," or "propitious occasion." This is what we could call
]{.calibre4}[[qualitative
time]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.^[[[55]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^
Naturally, we are not talking about two "types" of time, but two ways of
considering time. For instance, in St. Paul's writings,
]{.calibre4}[[kronoi]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ are generally periods of
time between two ]{.calibre4}[[kairoi]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.
]{.calibre4}[[Kairoi]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ are understood as the
moments when God intervenes in history in a special way. Therefore,
considering time in a "quantitative" or "qualitative" way, Christ
determines the "fullness of time," the fullness of history.]{.calibre4}

[When Christ began his public life he said, "The time is fulfilled
\[]{.calibre4}[[peplérotai ho kairos]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[\]"
(Mk 1: 15). Because ]{.calibre4}[[kairos]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ means
"qualitative time" (]{.calibre4}[[opportune]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
time), we can understand this text and others accordingly (i.e.,
Eph 1: 10), not merely in a strictly literal sense (i.e., the opportune
moment has come for the beginning of the public presentation of Christ).
We can also understand these writings in the sense that with the
Incarnation, qualitative time has reached its plenitude
(]{.calibre4}[[peplérotai]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[). The different
]{.calibre4}[[kairoi]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, or concrete moments of the
special intervention of God in history, have been completely
fulfilled.^[[[56]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Accordingly, the Incarnation stands as the ]{.calibre4}[[central point
of history]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ in the precise sense that it
determines a ]{.calibre4}[[qualitative]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ line of
demarcation between "the new" and "the old." In Christ, all human
history acquires its ]{.calibre4}[[center]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[: the
past is oriented and has meaning in him, and the future after Christ
draws its meaning and value with regard to
him.^[[[57]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}[[Christ is the
center of history]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ because in him the Incarnation
of divine eternity in human time has been carried out, conferring to
time a transcendental quality: the foundation of the past and the
future. Christ is "the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end"
(Rv 21: 6). In other words, the coming of Christ represents the fullness
of time because this event determines the center of history in a
qualitative sense.]{.calibre4}

[Christ's fulfillment of history has another meaning. We have shown that
he determines the "plenitude of quantitative time." In fact, "the time
had fully come" (Gal 4: 4). Although the literal sense seems to indicate
that the period of time or duration that the Father established for the
preparation of the Incarnation has reached its
end,^[[[58]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ we can also say that the
"plenitude of quantitative time" means the fulfillment of time that has
reached its end. Then, in what sense should we say that the Incarnation
is the end of time (the end of history)?]{.calibre4}

[Christ's fulfillment of chronological history (quantitative time)
obviously does not mean that history ended twenty centuries ago. Rather,
it means that ]{.calibre4}[[every historical moment after the
Incarnation sees Christ as the present, not the
past]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. In fact, "Jesus Christ is the same
yesterday and today and for ever" (Heb 13: 8). ]{.calibre4}[[This
contemporaneity]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of Christ with every historical
time after the Incarnation is not only that of Christ in his glorious
state because he lives forever, but also the contemporaneity of the
mysteries of his life, Death, and glorification truly present in the
mysterious (sacramental) life of the Church.]{.calibre4}

[It might seem, therefore, that ]{.calibre4}[[the time of the
Church]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, considered as the end of history, would
have to remain undefined forever. However, in reality we know that
history will have "another end." This will be the end of time when the
Lord will come again in the
]{.calibre4}[[Parousía]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, and it will represent an
undeniable novelty for the whole creation. But, this eschatological
novelty will not be an essentially new one.]{.calibre4}

[In the explanation and spreading of this interpretation of history,
Christ is the ]{.calibre4}[[center and the end]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ in
the previously mentioned sense (a center that has a conclusive character
but is not yet at its end). Oscar Cullmann has made an important
contribution to our understanding of these issues, particularly by means
of his ]{.calibre4}[[Christus und die Zeit]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (1946)
and ]{.calibre4}[[Heil als Geschichte]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(1964).]{.calibre4}

[Cullmann viewed the historical centrality of Christ as a key moment of
movement in a series of ]{.calibre4}[[progressive
reductions]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[: creation-mankind-people of
Israel-remainder of
Israel-Christ-Apostles-Church-mankind-creation.^[[[59]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Cullmann illustrated the ultimately conclusive character of this series
of terms by means of an apt analogy, saying:]{.calibre4}

> [In a war, the decisive battle could be held in the course of one of
> the first stages of the campaign, nevertheless, hostilities go for a
> long time yet. . . . This is exactly the situation in which we find
> the believer ]{.calibre4}[[vis-à-vis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ the New
> Testament. Revelation proclaims the fact that Christ has won the
> battle of universal salvation by means of his death on the cross,
> followed by his glorious Resurrection. The believer, therefore, has a
> certitude of faith that allows him to enjoy the results of this
> victory, to in some fashion participate in the sovereignty of God over
> time.^[[[60]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Cullmann's work acts as a vigorous challenge to the Bultmannian thesis,
for Cullmann emphasized the essential importance of historical facts in
revelation and salvation. Cullmann and Bultmann disagree as to whether
or not one can reduce salvific-historical events to myths. Some
Protestant errors prevent Cullmann from being clear on this question.
For example, in the above quoted text, one can observe a certain
reduction of revelation to a simple event with some forgetfulness of the
noetic essential dimension of the Word of God.]{.calibre4}

:::

::: mbppagebreak
:::

[[CHAPTER 3]{.calibre4}]{.calibre9}\
[[[REVELATION AND THE CHURCH]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre24}

[Having studied how God communicates with men through his incarnate
Word, we shall now see how divine revelation is preserved and
transmitted through time. Christ has entrusted this mission to the
Church: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them
in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you; and lo, I am
with you always, to the close of the age" (Mt 28: 19-- 20). This
teaching mission implies a special authority and assistance given to the
Church.]{.calibre4}

[[[I. The Transmission of Revelation in the Church and by the
Church]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[A causal relationship exists between revelation and the Church. On the
one hand, the Church is engendered by the Word of God; on the other
hand, even though the Church does not "produce" revelation, she
manifests it to people of all times. She guards and interprets
revelation with authority from Christ. Before studying this
inter-relationship, we need to consider the event that essentially
predetermines it: Revelation ended with the death of the
apostles.]{.calibre4}

[[[A. Revelation Ended with the Apostles]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[From the fundamental reality that Christ is the plenitude of
revelation, it logically follows---as was previously mentioned---that
"the Christian economy, it is the new and definitive covenant, which
will never pass away; and no new public revelation is to be expected
before the glorious manifestation of our Lord, Jesus Christ
(cf. 1 Tm 6: 14;
Ti 2: 13)."^[[[1]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Revelation has come to us through the testimony of the apostles, to
whom Christ transmitted the mission of announcing the Gospel to all
nations (cf. Mt 28: 19-- 20).]{.calibre4}

[Nevertheless, the apostles did not receive the plenitude of this
revelation before the Ascension of Jesus. In fact, the Lord told them,
"I have yet many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth;
for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he
will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He
will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you"
(Jn 16: 12-- 14). Therefore, following the Ascension, revelation
continued until the death of the apostles without compromising the truth
that Christ is the plenitude of revelation.]{.calibre4}

[The Holy Spirit's special assistance to the apostles---assistance that
we can call "constitutive" of revelation---is a characteristic that is
proper and exclusive to the ]{.calibre4}[[apostolic
times]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. In fact, it has been understood thus since
the beginning of the Church: "The apostles, in handing on what they
themselves had received, warn the faithful to maintain the traditions
that they had learned either by word of mouth or by letter
(cf. 2 Thes 2: 15); and warned them to fight hard for the faith that had
been handed on to them once and for all
(cf. Jud 3)."^[[[2]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ This text clearly
says ]{.calibre4}[[hapax paradotheisé]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, the Latin
translation of which is not only ]{.calibre4}[[semel
traditae]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (delivered at only one time) but
]{.calibre4}[[semel pro semper traditae]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(delivered once and
forever).^[[[3]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The fact that there is no other revelation after the apostles leads
St. Paul, inspired by God, to speak about the contents of revelation as
a ]{.calibre4}[[deposit]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(]{.calibre4}[[parathéké]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) (cf. 1 Tm 6: 20;
2 Tm 1: 14). It is as something delivered to someone in order to
preserve and guard
it.^[[[4]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[During patristic times there was no shortage of voices promoting the
existence of new "revelations" that needed to be added to the apostolic
tradition; voices that the Fathers fought firmly against, especially
St. Irenaeus.^[[[5]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The comment of
St. Vincent of Lerins about the text of 1 Timothy 6: 20 is well known.
He emphasizes that we have received the
]{.calibre4}[[depositum]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ through public
transmission. We are not its authors but its
guardians.^[[[6]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Moreover, the universal Magisterium of the Church has stated on several
occasions that there is no public revelation other than that transmitted
by the apostles.^[[[7]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ In this regard,
we would do well to remember, the condemnation in the decree
]{.calibre4}[[Lamentabili]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of the modernist thesis
that claims that revelation was not completed with the
apostles.^[[[8]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[[[B. The Church: Summoned and Engendered by the Word of
God]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[The Church primarily originates in God the Father, who sent his Son to
the world to be the Redeemer of men and head of the Church, whose
members are incorporated into him through the work of the Holy Spirit.
According to the well-known words of St. Cyprian, we say that the Church
of God, the Church of Christ, is "a people united by the unity of the
Father, of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (]{.calibre4}[[de unitate
Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti plebs
adunata]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[).^[[[9]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[This divine action of the foundation of the Church has been carried out
in Christ and through Christ. We will not discuss here arguments
concerning Christ's will to found the
Church.^[[[10]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Nevertheless, it is
interesting to remember that during Jesus' life, there is neither a time
nor a concrete and determined act that can be considered the moment of
the foundation of the Church. From a radical point of view, we might say
that the Church, as a mystery, was born at the moment of the
Incarnation. Yet, we can state that in its visible reality as the new
people of God, Jesus gradually founded the Church until the arrival of
the Holy Spirit in Pentecost.]{.calibre4}

> [For the Lord Jesus inaugurated his Church by preaching the Good News,
> that is, the coming of the kingdom of God, promised over the ages in
> the scriptures: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at
> hand" (Mk 1: 15; cf. Mt 4: 17). This kingdom shone out before men in
> the word, in the works and in the presence of Christ. . . . When
> Jesus, having died on the cross for men, rose again from the dead, he
> was seen to be constituted as Lord, the Christ, and as Priest for ever
> (cf. Acts 2: 36; Heb 5: 6; 7: 17-- 21), and he poured out on his
> disciples the Spirit promised by the Father
> (cf. Acts 2: 33).^[[[11]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[In this way, the process of the foundation of the Church coincides with
the fulfillment of the plenitude of revelation. The Church is summoned
and engendered by the words and human actions of Christ---these are
words and human actions of God: The word of Christ that initiates the
apostles into the secrets of the Father founds the Church, giving her
also the three powers of preaching, sanctifying and governing. The word
of Christ conferred upon the apostles the mission of inviting men to
faith and of incorporating them by means of Baptism into the society of
the Father and the Son in one and the same Spirit. . . . In a certain
way, we can, therefore, state that the Word summons and engenders the
Church.^[[[12]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The causal relationship between the Word and the Church is reflected in
the name ]{.calibre4}[[ekklésia]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, derived from
]{.calibre4}[[ekkalein]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (to summon). It is also
shown through the names used to name Christians in the New Testament,
such as ]{.calibre4}[[kletoi]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ ("called,"
1 Cor 1: 24; Rom 1: 6-- 7; Rv 17: 14) and
]{.calibre4}[[ekklektoi]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ ("the chosen,"
cf. Rom 8: 33; Col 3: 12; 2 Tm 2: 10).]{.calibre4}

[This announcement and the generation of the Church by the Word is a
constant reality. It belongs to the initial implantation carried out
immediately by Christ. This is seen with utmost clarity, for instance,
in the birth of the different local churches in apostolic times (cf.,
i.e., Acts 2: 41-- 42; 8: 12-- 14; 2 Cor 3: 3; Eph 1: 13). The expansion
of the Church coincides with the spreading of the Word: "The word of God
grew and multiplied" (Acts 12: 24); "the word of the Lord spread
throughout all the region"
(Acts 13: 49).^[[[13]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[When we say that the Church is summoned and engendered by the Word of
God, it is obvious that we are using the expression "Word of God" in its
fullest sense: not just to express its noetic contents, but also to
express it as being an efficacious force for transforming reality. It is
not, therefore, the simple "exterior preaching" of the gospel that
generates the Church, but this preaching combined with the interior
action of the Holy Spirit, which leads to faith and to the sacraments of
faith (cf. Mt 28: 19-- 20; Mk 16: 15-- 16; Acts 2: 38;
Rom 10: 14ff.).^[[[14]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[[[C. The Church Presents the Word of God to
Men]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

["God graciously arranged that the things he had once revealed for the
salvation of all peoples should remain in their entirety, throughout the
ages, and be transmitted to all
generations."^[[[15]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ This transmission
of Divine Revelation is accomplished in the Church by means of Sacred
Tradition and Sacred Scripture.]{.calibre4}

[[[1. Tradition and Scripture]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

> [The apostolic preaching, which is expressed in a special way in the
> inspired books, was to be preserved by an unending succession of
> preachers until the end of time. Therefore the Apostles, handing on
> what they themselves had received, warn the faithful to hold fast to
> the traditions which they have learned either by word of mouth or by
> letter (see 2 Thes 2: 15), and to fight in defense of the faith handed
> on once and for all (see Jud 3) (First Vatican Council, Dogmatic
> Constitution on the Catholic Faith, Chap. 3, "On Faith:"
> Denzinger 1789 (3008)). Now what was handed on by the Apostles
> includes everything which contributes toward the holiness of life and
> increase in faith of the peoples of God; and so the Church, in her
> teaching, life and worship, perpetuates and hands on to all
> generations all that she herself is, all that she
> believes.^[[[16]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[This transmission, or ]{.calibre4}[[tradition]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(]{.calibre4}[[paradosis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[), of revelation has,
therefore, as its object (]{.calibre4}[[obiectum
traditum]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) the entire reality of Christianity. The
gospel is understood not only as an announcement or word, but as saving
force according to St. Paul's assertion: The gospel is the force of God
(]{.calibre4}[[dynamis theou]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) to save all
believers (cf. Rom 1: 16).]{.calibre4}

[The whole Church is the subject of Tradition (]{.calibre4}[[subiectum
tradens]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) accomplished (]{.calibre4}[[actus
tradendi]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) by the whole life of the Church, which
we can, therefore, summarize in ]{.calibre4}[[Traditio
evangelii]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, which has as its constitutive
dimensions the preaching of the Word and sacramental
celebration.^[[[17]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The term ]{.calibre4}[[Tradition]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(]{.calibre4}[[Paradosis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[), aside from the wide
sense of ]{.calibre4}[[transmission]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[---which
corresponds to its etymological meaning---has a restricted sense in
theology: It is the ]{.calibre4}[[oral
transmission]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of revelation made by the apostles
and continued in many ways (including writing) from generation to
generation in the Church. This apostolic preaching was put into writing,
with the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, in the books of the New
Testament.^[[[18]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ In other words,
Divine Revelation, transmitted by the apostles, comes to us by means of
Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition (understood in a strict
sense).^[[[19]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Unquestionably, "the Sacred Scriptures are the preeminent documents of
apostolic preaching. Due to the cause and virtue of divine inspiration,
they have a 'special title' of quality, unique in its gender, which
confers to the sacred books a privileged and irreplaceable function in
the transmission of
revelation."^[[[20]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ In fact, the
inspired books are the Word of God themselves, not merely human writings
narrating the apostolic preaching (as in the case of the post-apostolic
texts). "Everything asserted by the inspired authors or sacred writers
must be held to be asserted by the Holy
Spirit."^[[[21]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Therefore, the temporal priority of Tradition above Sacred Scripture
does not exclude the latter's preeminence in the above sense.
Additionally, the existence of Scripture does not exclude the need for
Tradition, not only for the purpose of knowing which books are inspired
by God, but also for the transmission of the whole Divine Revelation. In
this sense, we speak about ]{.calibre4}[[Traditio
interpretativa]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ when Tradition transmits something
that is already contained in the Bible. If it is explicitly stated in
Scripture, the interpretative Tradition is named ]{.calibre4}[[Traditio
declarativa]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[; if it is only implicitly contained,
then we speak about ]{.calibre4}[[Traditio
inhaesiva]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. Tradition is considered
]{.calibre4}[[constitutive]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ when it transmits what
is in no way contained in the inspired
books.^[[[22]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ In reality, the
existence or nonexistence of revealed truths that are not stated in
Scripture is a question that is open to many theological opinions. In
any case, Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition are so intimately and
essentially linked that by studying their reciprocal relationship, one
can reach a complete knowledge of Scripture and Tradition.]{.calibre4}

[An essential characteristic of Tradition is that it is a
]{.calibre4}[[living]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ reality. In fact, as
explained by the Second Vatican Council:]{.calibre4}

> [The Tradition that comes from the apostles makes progress in the
> Church, with the help of the Holy Spirit. There is a growth in insight
> into the realities and words that are being passed on. This comes
> about in various ways. It comes through the contemplation and study of
> believers who ponder these things in their hearts (cf. Lk 2: 19, 51).
> It comes from the intimate sense of spiritual realities that they
> experience. And it comes from the preaching of those who have
> received, along with their right of succession in the episcopate, the
> sure charism of truth. Thus, as the centuries go by, the Church is
> always advancing toward the plenitude of divine truth, until
> eventually the words of God are fulfilled in
> her.^[[[23]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Tradition, therefore, is not a simple repetition; it is something that
"advances" (]{.calibre4}[[proficit]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[). Although
Revelation has ended, the interpretation that gives it its meaning has
not been closed: "'Revelation' has finished, but not its binding
interpretation."^[[[24]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[We have before us, therefore, authentic intellectual
]{.calibre4}[[progress]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, but the progress is in
the understanding of the ]{.calibre4}[[depositum]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
because what progresses is "the Tradition of apostolic origin;" "Nothing
can exist that does not derive from the apostles. Nothing should be
taken away from what they have handed
on."^[[[25]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Therefore, revelation, completed and concluded with the deaths of the
apostles, comes to people of all times, not as a simple remembrance of
the past, but as a living and operative reality as Christ lives and
operates in his Church: "Lo, I am with you always, to the close of the
age" (Mt 28: 20).]{.calibre4}

[For every person, Revelation is the Word of God that communicates
knowledge and salvation. So it is today; Revelation is for everyone a
]{.calibre4}[[personal encounter]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ with the God who
saves. This encounter takes place ]{.calibre4}[[in the
Church]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ because it is the Church, and not
individuals as such, to whom Christ has entrusted the Word of God: "The
doctrine of the faith which God has revealed is put forward . . . as a
divine deposit committed to the spouse of
Christ."^[[[26]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ "Sacred Tradition and
Sacred Scripture make up a single sacred deposit of the Word of God,
which is entrusted to the
Church."^[[[27]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Tradition is, in this sense, the whole life of the Church. Obviously,
not every manifestation of this life or every doctrine that may be found
in the Church's past belongs to Tradition. This means that not
everything that is said or done (and has been said or done) in Christian
communities is of apostolic origin and therefore, binding for the Church
herself. The Church has ]{.calibre4}[[criteria of
Tradition]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. The fundamental criteria were
summarized by St. Vincent of Lerins in the fifth century: universality,
antiquity, and
unanimity.^[[[28]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[One may determine whether or not a doctrine fulfills these
characteristics in the ]{.calibre4}[[Magisterium of the
Church]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, the teachings of the
]{.calibre4}[[Fathers of the Church]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, the
]{.calibre4}[[liturgy]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, and the
]{.calibre4}[[common opinion of the
faithful]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.^[[[29]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Ecclesiastical writers are named ]{.calibre4}[[Fathers of the
Church]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ by meeting these characteristics: orthodox
doctrine, holiness, antiquity, and approval of the
Church.^[[[30]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The teachings of the
Fathers constitute a privileged testimony of Tradition because of their
antiquity and proximity to the apostolic times. In the words of the
Second Vatican Council, "the sayings of the Holy Fathers are a witness
to the life-giving presence of this
Tradition."^[[[31]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Naturally, not all statements of the Fathers on matters of faith are
expressions of apostolic Tradition. In order to recognize them as such,
these statements need to have the moral unanimity of the other Fathers.
Such moral unanimity can also be recognized based on the concordance of
a small number of the Fathers if they had much authority and influence
in the Church. In some cases, even the testimony of one Father may
constitute a sure criterion of Tradition if he exercised a significant
role in developing that issue. For instance, this is the case of
St. Anastasius with regard to the doctrine of the Trinity, and St. Cyril
of Alexandria with regard to Christological
matters.^[[[32]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Finally, recalling
that the primary and fundamental function of Tradition is the
interpretation of Sacred Scripture, the Church considers as infallible
the unanimous ]{.calibre4}[[consensus Patrum]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ in
their interpretation of biblical
texts.^[[[33]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[[[2. Tradition and the Magisterium]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[The totality of the Church, which has received the deposit of
revelation, lives from it and transmits it from the beginning.
Nevertheless, the apostles, who had a particular and more intense
knowledge of the mystery of Christ (cf. Mt 13: 11; 16: 18; Mk 9: 31)
received from the Lord the special mission of preaching the gospel: "All
authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and
make disciples of all nations" (Mt 28: 18-- 19).]{.calibre4}

[In addition to the permanent assistance of the Lord in the exercise of
their mission, the apostles also received the help of the Holy Spirit
(cf. Jn 14: 15-- 17; 15: 26; 16: 13). Further, among the apostles, Peter
]{.calibre4}\
[ received the special mission of ]{.calibre4}[[confirming his
brothers]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
(cf. Lk 22: 32).^[[[34]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The apostles faithfully carried out their teaching function
(]{.calibre4}[[magisterium]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[) (cf. Acts 2: 32;
5: 14) with an ]{.calibre4}[[authority recognized]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
from the start in the primitive community of disciples, who "devoted
themselves to the apostles' teaching" (Acts 2: 42).]{.calibre4}

[This mission was later transmitted by the apostles to their successors
(cf. Acts 20: 25-- 27; 2 Tm 4: 6; Ti 1: 5). Thus, the Second Vatican
Council explained: "That divine mission, entrusted by Christ to the
apostles, will last until the end of the world (cf. Mt 28: 20), since
the Gospel they are to teach is for all time the source of all life for
the Church. And for this reason the apostles, appointed as rulers in
this society, took care to appoint
successors."^[[[35]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The episcopal
order, which is constituted by the bishops (the successors of the
apostles), carries out this apostolic succession. The bishops are
]{.calibre4}[[subject]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ within the magisterial
function of the Church, which is carried out in communion with the
successor of Peter, the Roman
pontiff.^[[[36]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Even though all members of the Church have the mission to transmit the
gospel, ]{.calibre4}[[authenticity]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ is a
fundamental and exclusive characteristic of the episcopal Magisterium:
"But the task of giving an authentic interpretation of the Word of God,
whether in its written form or in the form of Tradition, has been
entrusted to the living teaching office of the Church
alone."^[[[37]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The exclusive teaching authority of the Church in the
]{.calibre4}[[authentic]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ interpretation of the
Word of God does not mean that others cannot interpret revelation in an
"authentic way," if we understand authentic as "genuine," "according to
the truth." It is obvious, for instance, that theologians have carried
out and may carry out valuable and genuine interpretation of Sacred
Scripture and Tradition. Actually, the
]{.calibre4}[[authenticity]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ that is exclusive and
proper to the Magisterium lies in the Magisterium's function of
interpreting revelation according to
]{.calibre4}[[authority]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. It means that "the
authentic Magisterium has authority," but not the simple authority of
one who "possesses a science" ("scientific authority") but the same
]{.calibre4}[[authority of
Christ]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.^[[[38]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^
This authority, therefore, obliges the faithful in all
conscience.^[[[39]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The Second Vatican
Council is quite clear on this question: The bishops are
]{.calibre4}[[doctores authentici seu auctoritate Christi
praediti]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ (authentic teachers, or rather, teachers
endowed with the authority of
Christ).^[[[40]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The ]{.calibre4}[[authority]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ with which the
Magisterium transmits and interprets the Word of God does not in any way
imply that the Magisterium of the Church substitutes for the source of
Revelation (God himself still speaking to men through Sacred Scripture
and Tradition) as several contemporary Protestant authors have
claimed.^[[[41]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ The Second Vatican
Council taught: "This Magisterium is not superior to the Word of God,
but is its servant. It teaches only what has been handed on to it.
]{.calibre4}\

[At the divine command and with the help of the Holy Spirit, it listens
to this devotedly, guards it with dedication and expounds it
faithfully."^[[[42]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[As has been mentioned before, the subjects of the Magisterium---the
bishops---receive a ]{.calibre4}[[participation]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
in the same authority of Christ in the sacrament of holy orders, through
which apostolic succession is carried out. Its authority is, therefore,
of a sacramental-charismatic nature, not a scientific-human one, and its
exercise depends upon the assistance of the Holy Spirit. Through
episcopal orders, in fact, bishops receive their ]{.calibre4}[[carisma
veritatis]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.^[[[43]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^
Due to the divine nature of magisterial authority, the Church teaches
that the Magisterium of the Church is infallible when it is fully
exercised with an ]{.calibre4}[[infallibility]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
that participates in divine infallibility.]{.calibre4}

[The proper ]{.calibre4}[[object]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of the
Magisterium is, therefore, the transmitted or written Word of God. This
object is traditionally described in several ways pertaining to the
contents that can be summarized in the following expression of patristic
origin: ]{.calibre4}[[res fidei et morum]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, matters
of faith and
morals.^[[[44]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The authority of the Magisterium in the exposition and interpretation
of the contents of the Word of God---that is, of revealed truths---also
holds regarding other truths that, although they have not been
explicitly revealed, are necessary in order to teach and defend revealed
truth. It is the Church's duty to indicate the elements in a
philosophical system which are incompatible with her own Faith. In fact,
many philosophical opinions---concerning God, the human being, human
freedom and ethical behaviour---engage the Church directly, because they
touch on the revealed truth of which she is the
guardian.^[[[45]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Thus, a distinction
is drawn between ]{.calibre4}[[primary objects]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of
the Magisterium, which are ]{.calibre4}[[formally]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[
revealed truths (explicitly or implicitly), and ]{.calibre4}[[secondary
objects]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, which are truths that are not contained
in Revelation but are necessary to duly expose and defend the deposit of
revelation. Some authors call these issues
]{.calibre4}[[virtually]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ revealed
truths.^[[[46]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The ]{.calibre4}[[modalities of exercise]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of the
Magisterium are manifold, but they can be summarized into two principal
orders: the ]{.calibre4}[[ordinary Magisterium]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[,
which is the individual teaching of each bishop, and the
]{.calibre4}[[solemn Magisterium]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[, which is made
up of the councils or the pope when he teaches ]{.calibre4}[[ex
cathedra]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[.]{.calibre4}

[The clear significance of this is that the magisterium is an integral
part of the Church's Tradition; and, at the same time, the authentic
means of interpreting this Tradition.]{.calibre4}

[Tradition is the transmission not only of doctrine, but also of the
whole reality of the Church. Consider again the words of the Second
Vatican Council: "The Church, in her doctrine, life, and worship,
perpetuates and transmits to every generation all that she herself is,
all that she believes."^[[[47]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ Thus,
we must understand that the apostolic succession, from the apostles to
the bishops and from St. Peter to the bishop of Rome, is a succession
that obeys the will of Christ in his founding of the
Church.^[[[48]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^ This is the sacramental
form of Tradition and its unifying
presence.^[[[49]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[Consequently, in the transmission of divine revelation, we find three
intimately related realities: "Sacred tradition, Sacred Scripture and
the teaching authority of the Church, in accord with God's most wise
design, are so linked and joined together that one cannot stand without
the others, and that all together and each in its own way under the
action of the one Holy Spirit contribute effectively to the salvation of
souls."^[[[50]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[[[D. The Apostolic Church and the Post-Apostolic
Church]{.calibre4}]{.bold}]{.calibre9}

[In the apostles' mission, there was an element that ]{.calibre4}[[could
not be transmitted]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[. This element was the
constitution of the ]{.calibre4}[[depositum]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ by
the special assistance of the Holy Spirit that Christ promised to them.
In that sense, regarding the revelation-Church relationship, there is a
certain ]{.calibre4}[[discontinuity]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ between
apostolic and post-apostolic time, between the apostolic and
post-apostolic Church.]{.calibre4}

[Protestant theology has argued that this discontinuity could justify
the negation of the principle of Tradition in the post-apostolic Church.
Consequently, a distinction has been drawn between the apostolic
Tradition, which we can reach only by Scripture, and the post-apostolic
Tradition, which would be, therefore, a non-binding
tradition.^[[[51]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[O. Cullmann advocated this Protestant theory of the discontinuity
between the apostolic and the post-apostolic Church (between "the
apostles' Church" and "the bishops' Church"). He claims that the
discontinuity arises from the fact that the principle of Tradition,
which the apostolic Church had been living, lost its validity with the
birth of Scripture. According to Cullmann, the proof of this argument
lies in the organization of the ]{.calibre4}[[biblical
canon]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ by the same Church in the second century.
"Upon establishing the ]{.calibre4}[[principle]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ of
a canon, the Church has recognized that ]{.calibre4}[[from that moment
on]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ tradition was not a criterion of truth
anymore."^[[[52]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[History tells a different story. When the Church established the
biblical canon, she did not find it expedient to expunge the principle
of Tradition from her life. As a matter of fact, Tradition was one of
her most valuable resources when recourse to Sacred Scripture did not
seem sufficient to teach the full deposit of revelation.]{.calibre4}

[Further, the recognition of the authority of the writings of the New
Testament cannot be reduced to a special moment; rather, it is the
product of the process of the transmission of the Church's living
Tradition. This process does not pertain solely to the second century.
In reality, from her earliest days (even during the lives of the
apostles), the Church recognized an absolute authority in some writings
that were considered
"apostolic."^[[[53]{.calibre4}]{.calibre32}]{.small}^]{.calibre4}

[The Church's fidelity to the apostolic faith ensures that the Church of
all times is the ]{.calibre4}[[same]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[ Church of
Christ and the apostles. This fidelity, with the help of the Holy
Spirit, is guaranteed by Scripture and, in an inseparable way, by
Tradition (with the Magisterium as an interpreter of Tradition itself).
Hence, the discontinuity between the apostolic and post-apostolic Church
is not a total discontinuity. It is more a continuity than a
discontinuity; ]{.calibre4}[[the apostolic and post-apostolic Church are
the same]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[: the Church of Christ. They impart the
same Revelation, the same Word of God that the apostles faithfully
received from Christ and the Holy Spirit through a special charism
(]{.calibre4}[[inspiration]{.calibre4}]{.italic}[). The same Word
resounds in the Church of all times due not only to Scripture, but also
and inseparably to Tradition and the Magisterium.]{.calibre4}

[Finally, it is interesting to observe that "the insistence about
